chapterTitle: Do Nudges Last Forever? Perhaps in Sweden

facts.claim: Sweden's 2000 launch presented 456 funds from 72 companies to about four million savers.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the large catalog made the premium-pension allocation an unusually complex mass-market choice.
facts.commonError: Participants chose among a short curated list of fewer than ten funds.
facts.whyWrong: The launch menu contained hundreds of funds.

facts.claim: Cronqvist and Thaler found actively selected Swedish portfolios were generally costlier and less diversified than the default.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because advertising and recent returns attracted attention toward concentrated, higher-fee options.
facts.commonError: Active choosers reliably earned a diversification advantage over delegators.
facts.whyWrong: The observed portfolio characteristics pointed in the opposite direction.

facts.claim: The Seventh AP Fund managed the Premium Savings Fund for people who made no active selection.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a centralized default provided an investable allocation when savers delegated the decision.
facts.commonError: Nonchoosers left their premium-pension contributions in cash.
facts.whyWrong: Their money entered the state-run default fund.

facts.claim: Almost two thirds of eligible savers made an active choice in the launch year.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because government communication and private advertising framed active management as expected and responsible.
facts.commonError: The presence of a default caused nearly everyone to delegate immediately.
facts.whyWrong: The campaign against passive acceptance outweighed the default for the initial cohort.

facts.claim: Fund companies spent about 65 million US dollars advertising during the initial Swedish choice round, with spending falling below 10 million by 2003.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the collapse in promotion reduced salience and coincided with much lower active choice among later entrants.
facts.commonError: The menu attracted the same engagement without marketing.
facts.whyWrong: Active selection fell sharply as campaign intensity faded.

facts.claim: The original system let savers divide their allocation among one to five funds.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the rule encouraged portfolio construction from a hundreds-fund menu rather than one simple selection.
facts.commonError: Every active saver had to select exactly one fund.
facts.whyWrong: The design explicitly permitted multiple funds up to five.

facts.claim: Later cohorts entered the default at much higher rates than the 2000 cohort.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because with less advertising and public attention, inaction again became the path of least resistance.
facts.commonError: The culture of active pension management strengthened automatically over time.
facts.whyWrong: New-entrant active choice declined after launch.

facts.claim: Early active choices remained sticky even after the original promotional environment disappeared.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because review required attention and effort, so savers treated a one-time portfolio as a set-and-forget decision.
facts.commonError: Active choosers continuously rebalance because they rejected delegation once.
facts.whyWrong: Initial activeness did not imply ongoing monitoring.

facts.claim: An age-adjusted default reduces equity exposure as retirement approaches.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a lifecycle allocation automatically changes risk when the saver may not revisit the portfolio.
facts.commonError: A good retirement default should hold the same asset mix at every age.
facts.whyWrong: Capacity to absorb market loss changes with the remaining investment horizon.
